TWO FINDINGS ON THE DRILL DESIGN (DoD 4). Neither is a production defect; both are reported because the step text told me to report rather than paper over.

FINDING 1 — THE PLAN'S RESTORE PROOF IS UNSATISFIABLE ON THIS ROW. Step 3 says "the path is TRACKED, so an empty `git diff` on it is a valid restore proof." True of the path in the abstract, false at this point in the flow: step 2's delivered fix lives in the working tree, so `git diff` reads `58 2` before, during and after every drill. An EMPTY `git diff` here would prove the opposite of restoration — that the fix itself had been destroyed. The instrument has to distinguish "restored to the PRE-DRILL state" from "restored to HEAD", and `git diff` cannot: it only ever measures against HEAD.

I used SHA256 equality against an out-of-tree pre-drill backup instead, taken in a call separate from each restore, with a two-sided comparator I verified fires on a wrong hash before trusting it. Generalisable: `git diff --exit-code` is a valid restore proof ONLY when the mutated path is clean at drill time. On a row that drills a path it has already edited — which is every red-first row that drills its own fix — the pre-drill hash is the only anchor.

A related trap I hit and corrected: `sha256sum` on a Windows path prefixes its output line with `\` (escaped-filename form), so a naive `cut -d' ' -f1` comparison of a repo-relative path against a `%TEMP%` path reports a false MISMATCH on identical bytes. First run said RESTORE FAILED on two identical `a7dfce23…` hashes. Strip the escape before comparing.

FINDING 2 — HALF (b) IS UNOBSERVABLE AS WRITTEN, AND BOTH SPECIFIED MUTATIONS RED AT THE WRONG LINE.
(i) The "BLOCKED-card arms" are not arms. The goal.create census and the `cr.liveboard.missing.goal.create` project.activate assertions live INSIDE the same single `it(...)` as the dispatch assertions — there is exactly one test in that describe block. One arm cannot half-fail, so "(b) the BLOCKED-card arms STAY GREEN" has no measurement at test granularity. Its observable form is WHICH LINE the arm dies on.
(ii) Both specified mutations make the whole frame unreadable, so the arm dies at the FIRST card lookup (:243), never reaching the named `cr.liveboard.dispatch.approval.decide` assertion at :254. Cause is production's deliberate fail-closed design, not fixture coupling: `entryOf` -> null (live-planning-authorities.ts:175 `runId !== mapKey`, :179 `goalRef !== ownValue(goalRefs, runId)`) -> `materialByRun` null -> `bindPlanningAuthorities` false -> `frameOfSurface` returns `unreadable()` with ZERO steps (live-board-feed.ts:293-295). The module documents the intent at :194-195: "refuses the frame whole rather than binding the half it could read."

So as specified, the drill proves the fixture is sensitive to the material being WELL-FORMED, which is a weaker property than the one the step wanted — it cannot distinguish "the control is gated on this run's binding" from "the frame refuses to parse at all."

DRILL 3 is what closes that gap, and it is the shape I would recommend for any future drill against this seam: keep the map VALID so the frame parses, and move the material to a DIFFERENT run that is itself properly bound. Production accepts the map, both cards render, the BLOCKED assertions execute and pass, and the arm dies at :260 on `Unable to find an accessible element with the role "button" and name /^Dispatch /u` — the named assertion, with (a) and (b) both observed. That pins the arm to the PER-RUN binding rule rather than to frame parseability.

The underlying rule: to drill a per-item gate, mutate WHICH ITEM is bound, not WHETHER the container is valid. A container-invalidating mutation reds everything downstream and cannot discriminate the gate from its own precondition.
